title: When the requirements change
objectives: Extend working code when the interviewer adds a requirement part-way.

screens.title: A desk ledger
screens.prose: A small desk records its trades. Prices are whole £. After a contest you upsolve the problems you missed. Here the interviewer adds rules while it runs. First the simplest question.
screens.question: What is the position after the three trades?

hints.text: Which trades add to the position, and which take away?
Buys add and sales subtract.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buys add to the position and sales subtract.

byKey.all: You added the sale as if it were a buy. A sale takes shares away.
byKey.sold: You gave the quantity of the sale. The position is what is left after it.

explain.text: Signed quantities add up: buys are positive and sales negative. $100 + 100 - 150 = 50$ shares remain.

screens.title: Stage 1: positions
screens.prose: Start small. The ledger keeps one running position per symbol. Write it so that adding a rule later is easy.

params.title: Stage 1: Ledger()
lines: trade(symbol, qty): qty is signed, positive for a buy.
position(symbol): shares held, 0 if never traded.

screens.question: Write `Ledger` with `trade(symbol, qty)` and `position(symbol)`.

widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests: a buy then a sale, two symbols and a symbol never traded.

hints.text: What does the ledger need to remember?
One number per symbol.
Keep a dict from symbol to position. `trade` adds `qty`, `position` reads it with a default of 0.

feedback.correct: A dict of positions is all stage 1 needs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 buys 100 and sells 40, so 60 remain.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has two symbols and one never traded. A symbol never traded has position 0.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 sells everything: the position is 0.

explain.text: A dict from symbol to position is the whole state. `.get(symbol, 0)` handles a symbol never traded.

screens.title: Average cost
screens.prose: Now the desk wants profit. By average cost, the two buys cost £11 a share: $(100 \times 10 + 100 \times 12) / 200 = 11$. A sale realises quantity times (price minus average cost).

state.caption: Average cost after the two buys: £11

screens.question: What does the sale of 150 at £13 realise, in £?

hints.text: Which price do you subtract?
The average cost, £11, not one of the buy prices.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the average cost from the sale price, then multiply by the quantity sold.

byKey.first: You used the first buy, £10. The cost is the average of both buys, £11.
byKey.last: You used the last buy, £12. The cost is the average of both buys, £11.

explain.text: The average cost of the 200 shares is £11. Each of the 150 sold realises $13 - 11 = 2$, so the total is £300.

screens.title: Stage 2: average cost
screens.prose: The interviewer adds prices. The starter is stage 1 with the new signatures stubbed. Keep the old call valid: the stage 1 test is the last hidden test.

params.title: Stage 2: more on Ledger
lines: trade(symbol, qty, price=0): old calls must still work.
avg_cost(symbol): average price of the shares held, 0.0 if none.
realised(symbol): profit from sales so far.
A sale realises qty * (price - average cost).
Selling more than held raises ValueError.

screens.question: Add `avg_cost` and `realised` to `Ledger`.

tests.setup: L = Ledger(); L.trade('ABC', 5, 10); L.trade('ABC', -5, 8); L.trade('ABC', 5, 20); L.trade('ABC', -2, 22)

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. They include the stage 1 test with no price, an oversell and a buy of one share.

hints.text: What must be stored besides the position?
The average cost, and the profit made so far.
On a buy, the new average is $(\text{held} \times \text{avg} + qty \times price) / (\text{held} + qty)$. On a sale, add $qty \times (price - avg)$ to the profit.

feedback.correct: Position, average cost and profit per symbol; the default keeps old calls working.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the hook: 50 held, average £11, realised £300.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 sells everything: position 0, and the average goes back to 0.0.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 only buys. Realised stays 0 and the average is £12.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 buys again after a part sale: 120 shares at £10.5 on average.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 sells out and buys again, so the average restarts at £20.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is the stage 1 test. `trade` must still work without a price.

explain.text: A buy updates the average by weighting old and new shares. A sale leaves the average alone and adds its profit. The default `price=0` keeps stage 1 calls valid.

screens.title: The required argument
screens.prose: The interviewer says trades now carry a price. You change the signature to `trade(self, symbol, qty, price)` and run the stage 1 test, which calls `L.trade('ABC', 100)`.

params.title: Two signatures
lines: Required argument, which breaks old calls:
With a default, old calls still work:

screens.question: What happens to that test?

options.text: It fails: no price is passed, so Python raises `TypeError`.
It passes: Python reads a missing argument as 0, by default.
options.why: You assumed a missing argument becomes 0. Without a default, Python raises `TypeError`.

options.text: It passes: old tests do not see any new arguments at all.
options.why: Old calls are exactly what a new required argument breaks.

options.text: It passes, with the missing price filled in as `None`.
options.why: Python does not fill in `None`. A missing argument with no default is an error.

hints.text: How many arguments does the old call pass?
Two. The new signature asks for three.
Give the new argument a default, `price=0`, and the old call is valid again.

feedback.correct: A required new argument breaks every old call.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the arguments the old call passes.

byKey.b: Python has no automatic 0. It raises `TypeError` for the missing argument.
byKey.c: That is the trap. New required arguments break old callers.
byKey.d: No default is filled in. The call raises.

explain.text: A new required argument breaks every old call. A default value, `price=0`, keeps old calls valid and says what they meant. Running the old test first shows the break at once.

screens.title: First in, first out
screens.prose: The interviewer asks for FIFO: a sale uses the oldest shares first. On the same three trades, the sale of 150 takes the whole £10 lot. It then takes 50 shares of the £12 lot.
screens.question: What does the sale realise under FIFO, in £?

hints.text: Which lots does the sale use, and at what prices?
100 shares at £10, then 50 at £12.

feedback.correct: $300 + 50 = £350$. The £12 lot keeps 50 shares, so `avg_cost` is £12.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the sale across the lots, oldest first.

byKey.average: You used the average cost. FIFO uses the price of each lot sold.
byKey.newest: You sold only from the newest lot. FIFO takes the oldest shares first.

explain.text: The sale takes all 100 shares of the £10 lot and 50 of the £12 lot. That realises $100 \times 3 + 50 \times 1 = 350$. The 50 shares left cost £12 each.

screens.title: Stage 3: FIFO lots
screens.prose: Add a method choice. Keep a deque of lots, `[qty, price]`, oldest first. The starter is stage 2 with the new argument stubbed, and the hidden tests include every earlier one.

params.title: Stage 3: Ledger(method)
lines: fifo: a sale uses the oldest lots first.
fifo: avg_cost is the average of the lots still held.
The stage 1 and stage 2 tests must still pass.

screens.question: Add `method='fifo'` to `Ledger`, and keep the older tests passing.

tests.setup: L = Ledger(); L.trade('ABC', 5, 10); L.trade('ABC', -5, 8); L.trade('ABC', 5, 20); L.trade('ABC', -2, 22)
L = Ledger(method='fifo'); L.trade('ABC', 10, 50); L.trade('ABC', -4, 55); L.trade('ABC', 10, 40); L.trade('ABC', -12, 45)
L = Ledger(method='fifo'); L.trade('ABC', 5, 10); L.trade('ABC', -5, 8); L.trade('ABC', 5, 20); L.trade('ABC', -2, 22)

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. They are the stage 1 and 2 tests, four FIFO cases, then a buy of one share.

hints.text: Where do the old tests stand if you only add the new case?
They still run first. Add lots beside the old state, so nothing old changes.
Append `[qty, price]` on a buy. For FIFO, take from `lots[0]` until the sale is filled, adding `take * (price - lot price)`.

feedback.correct: A deque of lots serves FIFO, and the averages still work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is stage 2 behaviour: average cost still works without `method`.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 still needs the `ValueError` on an oversell.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is the stage 1 call with no price.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 is the FIFO hook: realised 350, and 50 shares left at £12.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 sells 250: the whole £10 lot and 150 of the £13 lot.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 sells across lots twice. FIFO realises 20.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 sells out, then buys again. The old lots are gone.

explain.text: Lots are kept in a deque, oldest first. A FIFO sale takes from the front, popping a lot when it is empty. The average method still uses its running average, so old tests pass.

screens.title: Which design absorbs the next change
screens.prose: The interviewer's next ask is short selling. A sale may take the position below 0, and a later buy covers it. Two designs are open.

state.caption: Lots remember what an average forgets

screens.question: Which design needs the fewest changes?

options.text: Keep a deque of signed lots, read by every rule.
Keep only a running average, which is the least state.
options.why: You counted state, not changes. An average cannot say which lot a sale used.

options.text: Rebuild a fresh list per symbol on every call.
options.why: You made each call slower and still need new rules. A deque already has the oldest lot first.

options.text: Copy the class and add short selling to the copy.
options.why: You duplicated the rules. Two copies must change together, so bugs double.

hints.text: What does each design remember about past trades?
Lots keep every purchase. An average keeps only a blend.
Both FIFO and a short position need to know which lot, or which side, a trade met.

feedback.correct: Lots keep what every rule needs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each design can still answer after a new rule.

byKey.b: A running average loses the lots, so FIFO and shorts would force a rewrite.
byKey.c: Rebuilding costs time on every call and adds no new information.
byKey.d: A copy doubles every future change.

explain.text: A deque of lots keeps the order and the price of every purchase. Average cost, FIFO and a short position are all read from it. A running average throws that information away.

screens.title: Absorbing a change
screens.prose:
The same moves worked in all three stages.

```python
def trade(self, symbol, qty, price=0):  # old calls still valid
    ...
Ledger(method='fifo')                   # new behaviour behind a name
```
screens.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Read the new requirement aloud and say what it adds
Give any new argument a default, so old calls stay valid
Put the new behaviour behind a name or an option
Run the old tests: they must still pass
Write a test for the new behaviour and run it
Rewrite the old method for the new rule and edit the old tests to match
lines.why: Editing old tests hides a break. They are the proof that nothing else changed.

hints.text: What comes first when a requirement arrives?
Say what changes, before you write anything.
Read it aloud, keep old calls valid, add the behaviour, run old tests, then test the new case.

feedback.correct: Read, keep old calls valid, add, run old tests, test the new.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Old tests are your safety net, so they run before the new ones.

byKey.d1: You edited the old tests to fit. That hides what the change broke.
byKey.left-out: Five steps belong. Only rewriting the old tests is wrong.

explain.text: Say what the change adds, keep old calls valid, and put the new behaviour behind a name. Run the old tests before the new ones, so a break shows at once.

screens.title: The first minute
screens.prose: Ten minutes remain. The interviewer says: sales must now use the oldest shares first. Your stage 2 ledger works.
screens.question: What do you say in the first minute?

options.text: Sales take the oldest lot, so I keep lots and rerun old tests.
I will start typing now, so I do not lose any time.
options.why: Silence hides your reading. The interviewer scores what you notice, not how fast you type.

options.text: I would rewrite the whole ledger around lots from scratch.
options.why: A rewrite spends the minutes and drops the old tests, your proof that nothing broke.

options.text: That needs more time than we have left, so I would skip it.
options.why: You treated the change as a blocker. Saying what it adds is the test.

hints.text: What does the interviewer want to hear?
What the change adds, what stays the same and what it costs.
Name the new data (lots), the promise (old calls and tests) and the order of work.

feedback.correct: Name the change, the promise and the order of work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Say what changes before you type.

byKey.b: Typing without a word hides your plan, and a wrong plan costs the minutes.
byKey.c: Extending keeps the old tests as proof. A rewrite throws them away.
byKey.d: Declining the change costs the marks. Extend it and name the cost.

explain.text: Interviewers score how you handle the change: you read it, keep old behaviour, name the cost, and extend. The cost here is storing lots instead of one average. Say it aloud before you code.

screens.title: Two methods, one desk
screens.prose: A desk trades: buy 20 at £30, sell 5 at £34, buy 10 at £36, sell 15 at £33. The risk team asks how the two methods differ.
screens.question: How much more does FIFO realise than average cost, in £?

widget.accept: 36: FIFO realises 65 and average cost realises 29

hints.text: Work out each method separately.
FIFO: the first sale uses £30 shares. The second sale uses the rest of that lot.
FIFO: $5 \times 4 + 15 \times 3 = 65$. Average: $5 \times 4 + 15 \times (33 - 32.4) = 20 + 9 = 29$. The difference is 36.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both realised profits, then subtract.

byKey.fifo: You gave the FIFO profit. The question asks for how much more it is than the average-cost profit.
byKey.avg: You gave the average-cost profit. Subtract it from the FIFO profit.

explain.text: FIFO sells the £30 shares both times: $5 \times 4 + 15 \times 3 = 65$. By average cost the second sale faces £32.4, so it realises 9 and the total is 29. The methods differ by £36.

ideas: When a requirement arrives, say what it adds, then extend the working code instead of rewriting it.
Give a new argument a default so old calls stay valid. Put new behaviour behind a name or an option.
Run the old tests first. Then test the new behaviour. Lots in a deque can serve average cost and FIFO alike.

quiz.question: Trades in one symbol: +30, -12, +5, -8. What is the position?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Buys add and sales subtract.

byKey.sizes: You added every size. Sales are negative.
byKey.flip: You flipped the sign. Positive trades are buys, so the position is positive.

quiz.question: Buy 40 at £9, then buy 60 at £14. What is the average cost per share, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each price by its quantity.

byKey.mean: You averaged the two prices. The larger buy counts for more.

explain.text: The cost is $40 \times 9 + 60 \times 14 = 1{,}200$ for 100 shares. That is £12 a share.

quiz.question: Buy 10 at £8, buy 10 at £11, then sell 5 at £12 under FIFO. What does the sale realise, in £?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. FIFO sells the oldest lot first.

byKey.newest: You used the £11 lot. FIFO uses the oldest, £8.
byKey.average: You used the average cost of £9.50. FIFO uses the price of the lot sold.

explain.text: The first 10 shares cost £8, and the sale of 5 comes entirely out of that lot. It realises $5 \times (12 - 8) = 20$.

quiz.question: Which signature keeps the old call `trade('ABC', 5)` valid once a price is added?

options.why: A required `price` makes the old call fail with `TypeError`.
Moving `price` first changes the meaning of every old argument.
A required keyword argument still breaks the old call.

feedback.correct: A default fills the missing argument.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The old call passes two arguments.

byKey.b: No default, so the old call raises.
byKey.c: The old arguments would land in the wrong places.
byKey.d: The keyword is required, so the old call still fails.

explain.text: Only a default makes the new argument optional, so old calls with two arguments stay valid.
